companyRankingLists.itemDescription:
Phillips 66, a major operator of refineries and gas stations, climbed 37 spots in the rankings on the back of soaring crude oil prices, which boosted its revenue by 53% to $175 billion in 2022.

  • In an effort to expand its already lucrative natural gas business—which generated $3.2 billion in profit in 2022—Phillips 66 acquired all the publicly available shares of pipeline company DCP Midstream, amassing an 87% equity stake.

  • In October 2022 Phillips 66 laid off 1,100 employees as part of CEO Mark Lashier’s attempts to find $500 million in cost savings by year-end.

  • As part of the oil company’s sustainability efforts, Phillips 66 has announced that it will convert a crude oil refinery in Northern California to a renewable fuels facility that will manufacture biofuels.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: As the world opened up in 2021, Phillips 66 bounced back; its revenue rose 75.4%, to $116 billion, boosted by the rebound in fuel consumption. As a major operator of refineries and gas stations, the company’s profit margins can be vulnerable when oil prices are particularly high, but Phillips was still able to produce $1.3 billion in profit. In April 2022, Mark Lashier, formerly president and CEO of the Chevron Phillips Chemical Company joint venture, succeeded Greg Garland as Phillips 66 CEO.

companyRankingLists.description: Total revenue for the world’s biggest companies fell 4.8% to $31.7 trillion this year—the first decline in half a decade.

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: It was a tumultuous year for Phillips 66, the Houston-based energy company. As lockdowns rippled around the globe, demand for transport fuels for cars and planes plunged, while losses mounted industrywide. Phillips 66 was no exception: The company lost $4 billion for the full year on a 40% drop in revenues. Like its peers, the company cut operating costs and slashed capital spending. The start of 2021, too, was rocky, as a crippling February storm in Texas hit operations in the state from refineries to pipelines.

image.title: G500-2020-061-Phillips 66
image.caption: Fuel pumps stand empty at a Phillips 66 gas station in Princeton, Illinois, U.S., on Wednesday, April 1, 2020. Even with the combination of some Canadian pullback, stripper wells going offline and announced shale cuts, that may not be enough to stop oil prices from going lower as demand craters and supply from OPEC means major increases in stockpiles in the second quarter. Photographer: Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images

companyRankingLists.itemDescription: Phillips 66 continued to expand in 2019, extending its network of pipelines. It announced an $8 billion joint petrochemical venture with Chevron and Qatar Petroleum, and pushed for an offshore export terminal in the Gulf of Mexico. The Houston-based refiner was not hiding its ambition: it wanted to go all-in on the U.S. shale boom. But relatively weak prices in 2019 helped push the company’s adjusted earnings down by about 34% from last year's figure, to $3.7 billion. Across the oil sector, 2020 started with a jolt. The January price spike gave way to the coronavirus-fueled price crash, which quickly led refineries to cut back production.

companyRankingLists.description: Global business is back. After limping through a worldwide financial crisis and economic slowdown, the 500 largest companies ranked by revenues shattered all sorts of performance records in 2013: They racked up combined revenues of $31.1 trillion, up 2.5% from 2012, and profits soared 27% to nearly $2 trillion. China’s 95 companies (up from 89 last year) posted $5.8 trillion in revenues. The U.S. has four fewer companies on the list than last year but remains (for now) the country leader, with 128 corporations on the list—including No. 1 Wal-Mart Stores—reporting $8.6 trillion in revenues.
